state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about this table as a journey. Each value of \( r \) is like a stop along the way. When you add a specific value of \( r \), you're taking a step forward in the journey. How does that change the value of \( f \)?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, so like... when r goes up by 1, the f value goes up by a certain amount? But I'm confused because the jump from 6 to 15 is 9, so I thought it would keep going up by 9 each time, which is why I got 24. Are you saying it doesn't work like that?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of each pair of \( r \) and \( f \) values as coordinates on a map. When you move from one point to the next, you're not always taking the same size step. Can you see how each step might be a different size in this journey?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses vague metaphors (journey, map) that don't directly address the linear-addition misconception, the student explicitly restates their misconception in Turn 2 without correction, and there's no evidence the student's understanding improves by the end.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use real-world analogies (journey, map, steps), these metaphors are vague and don't concretely ground the quadratic relationship in a meaningful everyday situation that would help the student understand why the differences aren't constant.
